lead: A thin semiconductor strip carrying current in a magnetic field develops a small voltage across its width: the field pushes the moving carriers to one side, so one edge becomes positive and the other negative. This is the Hall effect, and the voltage is proportional to the field. Hall sensors measure flux density, detect a magnet, count gear teeth, read the current in a wire without breaking the circuit, and find north in a phone compass. They are small, cheap, wear-free and work from DC to high frequency.
prereq: You need: sensitivity from the static characteristics of sensors, and the idea of drift current in a semiconductor.

sections.h3: The Hall effect and the Hall voltage

blocks.text: Take a thin rectangular plate of n-type semiconductor. Send a current I along its length. Apply a magnetic field B perpendicular to the plate face. Each electron drifting with velocity v feels the Lorentz force F = qv × B, which pushes it sideways towards one edge.

Charge piles up on that edge until the electric field it creates pushes back with equal force. That sideways field, measured as a voltage between the two side contacts, is the Hall voltage V<sub>H</sub>. The build-up takes picoseconds, so the sensor responds almost instantly.

blocks.where: V<sub>H</sub> is the Hall voltage in volts; R<sub>H</sub> is the Hall coefficient in m³/C; I is the control current in amperes; B is the flux density in tesla; t is the plate thickness in metres.
n is the carrier density in carriers per m³; e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the electron charge. For p-type material the sign of R<sub>H</sub> flips, so the Hall voltage reverses.

blocks.text: Two design facts follow. Thin plates give large V<sub>H</sub> because t is in the denominator. Low carrier density gives large R<sub>H</sub>. InSb with n around 2 × 10²² m⁻³ is about four to five times more sensitive than silicon with n around 10²³ m⁻³ at the same current, because its carrier density is lower. Its high electron mobility also keeps the plate resistance low. GaAs sits in between and drifts less with temperature.

sections.h3: Driving the plate and reading the output

blocks.text: The plate is driven by a constant current, not a constant voltage. With I fixed, V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub>(T) I B / t changes only through the small drift of R<sub>H</sub>; under voltage drive the plate resistance rises with heat, the current falls and the output drifts far more.

A practical sensor includes more than the plate. The Hall voltage is only a few millivolts, so a differential amplifier with high common-mode rejection sits beside it on the same chip. Many parts add a Schmitt comparator so the output is a clean digital switch.

items: Linear sensor: output is an analog voltage proportional to B, used for position and current measurement.
Threshold switch: output snaps high or low when B crosses a set level, used for proximity, gear-tooth counting and shaft speed.
Ratiometric output: the analog output scales with supply voltage, so the analog-to-digital converter should share that supply.

blocks.text: The amplifier itself is treated with signal conditioning (differential and instrumentation amplifiers). Two non-idealities always remain. Offset is the output with B = 0, caused by misalignment of the side contacts; it can be trimmed at manufacture or measured and subtracted. Temperature drift comes from R<sub>H</sub> and n changing with heat. Ratiometric output cancels supply error and chopper stabilisation cancels amplifier offset drift, but the drift of R<sub>H</sub> itself needs temperature compensation.

A Hall current sensor wraps a ferrite ring around the conductor and cuts a narrow air gap of length g into the ring. The current I in the wire sets up a field in the ring; with a high-permeability core almost all of the magnetomotive force appears across the gap, so the gap field is B = μ<sub>0</sub> I / g. A Hall plate sits in the gap. The wire is never broken, so the sensor measures DC and AC current with full electrical isolation.

blocks.where: B is the gap flux density in tesla; μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m; I is the conductor current in amperes; g is the gap length in metres. It assumes the core permeability is so high that the core itself needs almost no magnetomotive force.

blocks.text: In a closed-loop (compensated) sensor a secondary coil on the ring is driven until the gap field is zero, and the coil current, a known fraction of I, is the output. This removes the drift and nonlinearity of the plate and the core. Position and speed sensing use the same plate: a magnet on a moving part changes B, a linear sensor reads the distance, and a threshold switch facing a toothed wheel gives one pulse per tooth. In medical equipment Hall switches sense lid and door closure in infusion pumps and the rotor position of brushless motors in pumps and ventilators.

spec.aria: A Hall plate with current flowing to the right in a field into the page, electrons collecting on the top edge and a Hall voltage of 7.6 millivolts across the width; beside it a ferrite ring with a 2 millimetre gap around a cable carrying 50 amperes, giving 31.4 millitesla in the gap.

examples.question: An InSb Hall plate has Hall coefficient R<sub>H</sub> = 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C and thickness t = 0.1 mm. A control current I = 10 mA flows while the plate sits in a flux density B = 0.2 T. (a) Find the Hall voltage V<sub>H</sub>. (b) Find the sensitivity in volts per tesla.
steps: Convert to SI units: t = 0.1 mm = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m; I = 10 mA = 0.01 A.
V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub> I B / t = (3.8 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C × 0.01 A × 0.2 T) / 1 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Numerator: 3.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.01 × 0.2 = 7.6 × 10⁻⁷; divided by 1 × 10⁻⁴ m this gives 7.6 × 10⁻³ V = 7.6 mV.
(b) Sensitivity S = V<sub>H</sub> / B = 7.6 × 10⁻³ V / 0.2 T = 0.038 V/T = 38 mV/T (equal to R<sub>H</sub> I / t at this current).
examples.answer: The Hall voltage is 7.6 mV, and the sensitivity is 38 mV per tesla at 10 mA control current.
examples.check:
RH = 3.8e-4
I = 10e-3
B = 0.2
t = 0.1e-3
VH = RH * I * B / t
print(VH)
print(VH / B)

examples.question: The InSb plate of the first example (sensitivity 38 mV/T at 10 mA) sits in a 2 mm air gap of a ferrite ring clamped around a cable carrying 50 A DC. (a) Find the gap flux density. (b) Find the Hall voltage. (c) An amplifier of gain 500 follows the plate. Find the output and the scale in mV per ampere.
steps: Data: I = 50 A, g = 2 mm = 2 × 10⁻³ m, μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, S = 38 mV/T = 0.038 V/T.
(c) V<sub>out</sub> = 500 × 1.19 mV = 0.597 V. Scale = 0.597 V / 50 A = 11.9 mV per ampere.
examples.answer: The gap field is 31.4 mT, the Hall voltage 1.19 mV, and the amplified output 0.597 V, a scale of 11.9 mV/A.
examples.check:
import math
B = 4*math.pi*1e-7*50/2e-3
VH = 0.038*B
print(round(B, 4), VH, round(500*VH, 3), round(500*VH/50*1000, 1))

traps: Do not confuse the Hall coefficient R<sub>H</sub> (m³/C, a material property) with the sensitivity in V/T: sensitivity is R<sub>H</sub> I / t and also depends on current and thickness.
Thickness must be in metres. Leaving 0.1 mm as 0.1 in the formula gives an answer 1000 times too small.
For p-type material the Hall coefficient is positive, so the Hall voltage polarity reverses compared with n-type at the same current and field. Examiners like this sign question.

The Hall voltage appears across the two side contacts, perpendicular to both the current and the field. On the wrong pair of edges the Hall component is zero, but you still read the resistive IR drop of the plate, which is usually much larger than V<sub>H</sub>.

quiz.q: State the Hall effect in one sentence and give the formula for Hall voltage.
quiz.a: A current-carrying conductor in a transverse magnetic field develops a voltage across its width because the field pushes the moving carriers sideways. V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub> I B / t.

quiz.q: Why is a constant-current drive preferred over constant-voltage drive for a Hall plate?
quiz.a: With current drive I is fixed, so V<sub>H</sub> = R<sub>H</sub>(T) I B / t changes only through the smaller drift of R<sub>H</sub>. Under voltage drive, plate resistance rises with temperature, lowers I, and adds a much larger drift.

quiz.q: A silicon Hall plate has R<sub>H</sub> = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/C and t = 0.25 mm. Find V<sub>H</sub> at I = 5 mA and B = 0.5 T.
A gear with 40 teeth turns at 1800 rpm past a threshold Hall switch. What is the output pulse frequency?
quiz.a: Revolutions per second = 1800 / 60 = 30. One pulse per tooth per revolution, so f = 40 × 30 = 1200 pulses per second = 1.2 kHz.

quiz.q: A linear Hall sensor reads 2.500 V at B = 0 and 2.900 V at B = 100 mT, with a 5 V supply. An unknown field gives 2.650 V. Find the field and comment on the offset.
quiz.a: Sensitivity = (2.900 − 2.500) / 0.100 T = 4.0 V/T. Field = (2.650 − 2.500) / 4.0 = 0.0375 T = 37.5 mT. The 2.500 V quiescent output is the offset (half supply here); it must be subtracted before scaling, otherwise the reading is wrong by 625 mT if offset is ignored.

quiz.q: A clamp-on Hall current sensor reads 2 % low after the ring has been dropped and its 2.0 mm gap has opened to 2.04 mm. Explain the error and why a closed-loop sensor would not show it.
quiz.a: In an open-loop sensor B = μ<sub>0</sub> I / g, so the reading is inversely proportional to the gap: 2.0 / 2.04 = 0.980, a 2 % low reading for the same current. A closed-loop sensor drives its secondary coil until the gap field is zero; at zero field the output is the coil current, set by the turns ratio, so the gap length no longer sets the scale.

beyond: Not for the exam. Three-axis Hall chips with on-chip offset cancellation let a phone act as a compass, and coreless Hall sensors read electric-vehicle pack currents of hundreds of amperes. Search: integrated Hall magnetic sensors, closed-loop current transducer.
